foil

/FOYL/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Foil means to thwart, frustrate, or defeat a plan, attempt, or person.

The detective managed to foil the jewel thief's museum heist by quietly swapping the famous diamond for a worthless replica.

Example

The goalkeeper foiled the striker's clever chip shot with a desperate, last-second leap.

The striker made an attempt — a tricky shot at the goal — and the goalkeeper defeated that attempt at the final moment. Stopping someone's attempt from succeeding is exactly what foil means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

thwart: Thwart, like foil, means to stop a plan or attempt from succeeding — the two are near-twins. Thwart is the plainer, all-purpose word; foil carries the flavor of a scheme cleverly undone, the verb of detective stories and headlines. You can thwart anything; you foil a plot.

frustrate: Frustrate means to block someone's efforts so they fail, and it often suggests repeated blocking that wears a person down — it also names the feeling that results. Foil is cleaner and more final: one attempt, defeated. A frustrated plan keeps hitting walls; a foiled plan is finished.

derail: Derail pictures a train thrown off its tracks: a derailed plan goes wrong midway and cannot continue on course. Foil pictures an opponent defeated — someone's attempt is stopped from succeeding, often by someone else's countermove. Plans derail by accident; plots get foiled by an adversary.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

assist: to help a plan or person succeed

enable: to make something possible

Where it sits · how completely the plan is stopped

hinder → foil → quash

hinder vs. foil: To hinder a plan is only to slow it down; to foil it is to stop it from succeeding at all.

quash vs. foil: To foil a scheme is to defeat that one attempt; to quash it is to crush it so completely it can never be tried again.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — foil: from Old French fouler, "to trample, tread on" - the word came into English whole, with no separable prefix or suffix

Put it together: Foil traces back to an Old French word meaning "to trample." The picture is vivid: when you foil a plan, you flatten it underfoot before it can succeed.

Use the root in a new word: foil (the kitchen wrap): Kitchen foil is a different word altogether, from Latin folium, 'leaf.' Our foil, 'to defeat a plan,' came into English whole from Old French fouler, 'to trample' — flattening a scheme underfoot — and left no common English relatives behind.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Slightly formal - news & storytelling

In this course, foil is a verb only. You foil a plan, a plot, an attempt, or a person's efforts - it is the classic verb of detective stories and news headlines ("Guard foils robbery"). Its near-twin is thwart; both mean the attempt is defeated, not merely slowed.
